title: Two texts, one theme: the source texts and comparison tasks
subject: English Language
source: Written for english-language/y10 lesson 35 (Pupil PDF worksheet with the source texts (printable or for a drawing tablet))
intro: Lesson 35. Both texts are below. Use comparative connectives: similarly, likewise, whereas, however, in contrast.

passage.title: Text A: We Are Treating the Sea as a Bin
passage.byline: A modern article by a marine conservation diver
paras: Last summer, on a beach in Cornwall, I picked up a crisp packet. The best-before date printed on it was older than I am. It had been drifting for decades, faded but whole, and it will still be drifting long after I am gone.

We all know the pictures by now: the turtle tangled in netting, the seabird whose stomach is full of bottle tops. We share them, we sigh, and then we buy our lunch wrapped in three layers of plastic. One widely quoted estimate says that a rubbish lorry's worth of plastic enters the sea every minute. Even if the true figure were half that, it would be a disgrace.

The problem is not that plastic exists. It is that we use it for seconds and throw it into a system that keeps it for centuries. Rivers carry it to the coast; tides break it into fragments so small that fish mistake them for food; and those fish end up on our plates. The sea is handing our rubbish back to us, one meal at a time.

Some say that the ocean is too vast to harm, that one bottle cannot matter. But the ocean is not a bottomless pit. It is a living system, and we are part of it. Fishing communities already report smaller catches; reefs that once glowed with colour are turning grey.
There are answers. Refill schemes, deposit returns on bottles and bans on single-use bags have all cut litter where they have been tried. None of them needs a miracle, only the will to start.

I have dived in waters so clear you could read a newspaper on the seabed, and I have dived in waters choked with bags that drift like ghosts. We are not short of evidence; we are short of courage. If we keep treating the sea as a bin, we should not be surprised when it stops feeding us.
passage.source: Teacher-written modern article for TGA (the writer is invented).

passage.title: Text B: Letter from the Harbour Wall
passage.byline: A letter written in a nineteenth-century style
paras: I write from the harbour wall, where the fishermen land such silver harvests as would feed a city. The sea is a vast and generous storehouse, and I am persuaded that no labour of man could ever empty it.

You would laugh to see me, perched upon a coil of rope with my writing-case upon my knee, while the boats come in one after another, so laden that the water laps at their sides. The herring lie heaped upon the quay like coin in a miser's dream, and the women of the town gut and salt them faster than my eye can follow.

An old fisherman told me this morning that his grandfather took as many fish as he, and his grandson will take as many again. I do not doubt him. Providence has filled these waters with a bounty that renews itself with every tide, and the only limit upon our harvest is the number of our boats and the strength of our arms.

I confess that the sight fills me with a kind of pride. Here is the power of an industrious people: steam to carry the catch inland by night, ice to keep it sweet, and markets in every town that will buy it by morning.
Tomorrow I go out with the fleet, if the weather holds. Pray do not fear for me; the men assure me the sea is as gentle as a lamb this month.
passage.source: Teacher-written for TGA in a nineteenth-century style (the writer is invented).

questions.q: Rewrite as one comparative sentence: 'Text A is urgent. Text B is calm.'
questions.a: For example: 'Whereas Text A is urgent and alarmed, Text B is calm and confident.'

questions.q: Find one idea both writers share and one way their views differ.
questions.a: Both see the sea as a source of food; Text A fears we are destroying it, while Text B is 'persuaded that no labour of man could ever empty it'.

questions.q: Write one integrated comparative paragraph on 'human power over the sea'.
questions.a: For example: both writers present human power, but Text B celebrates it ('the power of an industrious people') whereas Text A shows it as destructive and calls for 'courage' to limit it.
